label: Foundations of Law and Mock Trial

lessons.title: Sources and Hierarchy of Law
body: American law has several sources, and they are ranked. At the top is the United States Constitution. Under it sit federal statutes, which are laws passed by Congress, and treaties made under the Constitution. Below those are federal regulations, which are detailed rules issued by executive agencies under authority a statute gives them. Each state has the same layers on its own level: a state constitution, state statutes, and state agency regulations. Cities and counties add ordinances, which are local laws that depend on powers the state grants.

There is a fifth source that runs alongside the written ones: judge-made law, often called common law. Where no statute covers a subject, courts decide disputes by reasoning from earlier decisions. Contract and tort law began largely this way, and many areas are still shaped by court decisions even where legislatures have added statutes. The principle of stare decisis tells courts to follow their own earlier decisions and those of higher courts in the same system. A decision from a higher court in the same jurisdiction is binding precedent. A decision from another jurisdiction is only persuasive.

When sources conflict, the higher one controls. The Supremacy Clause in Article VI makes the Constitution, federal statutes made under it, and treaties the supreme law of the land, so they override conflicting state law. In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Supreme Court held that it is the job of courts to say what the law is and that a statute contradicting the Constitution cannot stand. This power is called judicial review.

Consider a state statute that conflicts with a valid federal statute on the same subject. The federal statute prevails to the extent they conflict, a result lawyers call preemption. A state statute that conflicts with a federal regulation can be preempted too, as long as the regulation itself is authorized by a valid statute.

lessons.title: The Constitution and the Separation of Powers
body: The Constitution divides the national government into three branches. Article I gives legislative power to Congress, Article II gives executive power to the President, and Article III gives judicial power to the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts that Congress creates. The framers split power on purpose, because they feared that gathering lawmaking, enforcing, and judging in the same hands would invite tyranny.

The branches also check one another. The President can veto a bill, and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in each chamber. The Senate confirms the President's judicial and many executive nominees and must give advice and consent to treaties by a two-thirds vote. Congress can impeach and remove officials, with the House voting on impeachment and the Senate holding the trial. Courts can review whether a law or an executive act is constitutional, which is the power recognized in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

The case of Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) shows how this works. During a war and a threatened steel strike, President Truman ordered the government to seize steel mills. The Supreme Court held that he lacked the power, because neither the Constitution nor any statute authorized the seizure, and the President's job is to carry out laws rather than make them. The concurring opinion of Justice Jackson in that case is often used to describe a sliding scale: presidential power is strongest when backed by Congress, uncertain when Congress is silent, and weakest when the President acts against Congress.

A common mistake is to think that the President can make any rule by executive order. An executive order must rest on a power in the Constitution or in a statute. If it does not, a court can strike it down. Likewise, Congress cannot simply do the President's or the courts' jobs.

lessons.title: The Bill of Rights and Incorporation
body: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791. The First Amendment protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. The Second protects a right to keep and bear arms. The Fourth bars unreasonable searches and seizures and sets the standards for warrants. The Fifth covers grand juries for serious federal crimes, double jeopardy, the privilege against self-incrimination, due process, and just compensation for property taken by the government. The Sixth guarantees a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, the right to confront witnesses, and the assistance of counsel. The Eighth bars excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

Originally these limits applied only to the federal government. In Barron v. Baltimore (1833), the Supreme Court held that the Bill of Rights did not restrict state governments. After the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) said that no state may deprive a person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. Over the twentieth century the Court used that clause to apply most of the Bill of Rights to the states, a process called selective incorporation. In Gitlow v. New York (1925), the Court assumed that free speech was protected against state action. In Mapp v. Ohio (1961), it held that evidence obtained through an unreasonable search by state officers cannot be used in state courts, which is the exclusionary rule.

Some parts are contested. The Second Amendment is the clearest example. In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Court held that it protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense. Supporters see that right as basic to personal safety and equal to other constitutional rights. Critics emphasize public safety and the historic role of regulation, and they note that Heller itself said that some regulations, such as bans on possession by felons, remain valid. The law as of this writing is that the right is individual and applies to states, while the extent of permitted regulation continues to be litigated.
Rights are not unlimited even when they apply. Courts ask how strong the government's reason is and how closely the law fits it.

lessons.title: Federalism
body: Federalism is the division of power between the national government and the states. The national government has only the powers the Constitution lists, which are called enumerated powers. The Tenth Amendment says that powers not delegated to the nation, nor forbidden to the states, are reserved to the states or the people. States have a general power to protect health, safety, and welfare, often called the police power, which is why most criminal law, family law, and property law is state law.

The Constitution also gives Congress the power to make all laws that are necessary and proper to carry out its listed powers. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court held that Congress could create a national bank even though the Constitution does not mention banks, because the bank was a reasonable means to carry out listed powers like taxing and borrowing. It also held that a state could not tax the national bank, since the states cannot tax a federal institution out of existence.

The most important listed power in modern times is the power to regulate commerce among the states. The Court has read it broadly, but not without limit. In United States v. Lopez (1995), it held that the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded the commerce power, because carrying a gun near a school was not itself economic activity and the link to interstate commerce was too weak. The case shows that federal power has edges.

States are also protected from being drafted into federal service. In Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association (2018), the Court held that Congress may regulate private actors but may not command state legislatures to keep or pass particular laws. This is called the anti-commandeering principle.

People disagree about the right balance. Some argue that state control lets communities experiment and reflect local values. Others argue that national rules protect people from unequal rights depending on where they live. The courts decide the legal limits, while voters decide the policy.

lessons.title: Court Systems and Jurisdiction
body: The United States has two parallel court systems: the federal courts and the court system of each state. Most systems have three levels. Trial courts hear evidence, find facts, and apply law. Intermediate appellate courts review trial records for legal errors. A highest court, such as the Supreme Court of the United States or a state supreme court, decides the most important questions of law. In the federal system the trial courts are the district courts, the intermediate courts are the regional courts of appeals, called circuits, and the top court is the Supreme Court.

An appeal is not a new trial. Appellate judges generally accept the trial court's findings of fact and review whether the law was applied correctly. They read written briefs and hear short oral arguments. The Supreme Court controls most of its docket by granting petitions for certiorari, and by tradition it takes a case when four justices vote to hear it.

Jurisdiction means a court's power to hear a case. Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction. They can hear cases that raise a federal question, meaning the claim arises under the Constitution, federal statutes, or treaties. They can also hear cases between citizens of different states, called diversity cases, when the amount in dispute exceeds $75,000 and no plaintiff shares citizenship with any defendant. State courts are courts of general jurisdiction and hear most disputes. Personal jurisdiction is separate: a court needs a sufficient connection to the defendant, such as residence or purposeful contact with the state.

When a federal court hears a state-law claim under diversity jurisdiction, Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938) requires it to apply the state's substantive law. Consider a customer from Ohio who sues a Michigan company for $200,000 over a contract. A federal court may hear it under diversity jurisdiction, but it will apply the contract law of the appropriate state.

lessons.title: How a Civil Case Moves
body: A civil case begins when the plaintiff files a complaint, which states the facts and the legal claims, and serves it on the defendant with a summons. The defendant answers, admitting or denying the allegations and raising defenses. Before answering, a defendant may move to dismiss. Under Rule 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim asks whether, even if every fact in the complaint is true, the law gives the plaintiff a remedy. Courts do not weigh evidence at this stage.

Next comes discovery, the process by which each side obtains information from the other. Tools include interrogatories, which are written questions, requests for documents, and depositions, where a witness answers questions under oath outside the courtroom. Discovery is meant to avoid surprise and lets parties learn what evidence exists. It is limited to information relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case, and privileged material, such as attorney-client communications, is protected.

After discovery, a party may move for summary judgment under Rule 56. The court grants it when there is no genuine dispute about a material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. The judge asks whether a reasonable jury could find for the other side, and views the evidence in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion. Summary judgment is not a way to decide who is more credible.

If the case survives, it goes to trial. The Seventh Amendment preserves jury trial in federal civil cases at common law. After the verdict, the losing side may ask the judge to override it or order a new trial, and then may appeal to the court of appeals. Most civil cases never reach trial. They settle, meaning the parties agree to resolve the dispute, often after discovery reveals the strengths and weaknesses of each side.

lessons.title: How a Criminal Case Moves
body: A criminal case is brought by the government. Investigation may involve searches and seizures, which the Fourth Amendment limits. A search generally requires a warrant based on probable cause, meaning a fair probability that evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place, though courts recognize exceptions such as consent, items in plain view, and emergencies. An arrest also requires probable cause. Evidence found through an unconstitutional search is usually excluded from trial under the exclusionary rule.

Before police question a suspect in custody, they must give the warnings from Miranda v. Arizona (1966): the right to remain silent, that statements can be used against the suspect, and the right to a lawyer, including a free one. A statement obtained in violation of Miranda is generally not admissible in the prosecution's main case. The warnings are required only when there is custodial interrogation.

After arrest, the defendant makes an initial appearance, where the judge states the charges and addresses bail or release. For serious federal crimes, the Fifth Amendment requires an indictment by a grand jury, which decides whether there is probable cause to charge. Many states use a preliminary hearing instead. At arraignment the defendant enters a plea. The Sixth Amendment guarantees counsel, and Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) held that states must provide a lawyer to felony defendants who cannot afford one.

The large majority of criminal cases end in a plea bargain, where the defendant pleads guilty, often to a lesser charge or for a recommended sentence. Plea bargaining saves time but is also criticized for pressuring defendants, including innocent ones, to avoid the risk of a longer sentence. If the case goes to trial, the defendant has the right to a jury, to confront witnesses, to refuse to testify, and to be free from being tried twice for the same offense after an acquittal. A guilty verdict is followed by sentencing and may be appealed, but the government generally cannot appeal an acquittal.

lessons.title: Burdens and Standards of Proof
body: Two ideas are easy to confuse. The burden of persuasion is the duty to convince the fact finder, usually a jury, that a fact is true to the required degree. The burden of production is the duty to bring forward enough evidence on an issue so that it can be decided at all. If a party carries the burden of persuasion and does not meet it, that party loses on the issue.

The standard of proof says how convinced the fact finder must be. The lowest and most common is preponderance of the evidence, which means more likely than not, or just over fifty percent. It is the usual standard in civil cases, such as injury or contract disputes. A middle standard is clear and convincing evidence, which requires that the fact be highly probable. It is used for certain civil matters involving serious interests, such as in many states fraud claims, and for ending a parent's rights, where Santosky v. Kramer (1982) held that due process requires at least that level of proof. The highest standard is proof beyond a reasonable doubt, which the Constitution requires in criminal cases. In re Winship (1970) held that this standard is required, and extended it to juvenile delinquency proceedings that can lead to loss of liberty.

In a criminal case the prosecution bears the burden of proving every element of the charged offense beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant does not have to prove innocence. If the defendant raises an affirmative defense, such as self-defense in many states, rules differ about who bears the burden of persuasion on it, so the law of the state matters.

Consider a case where a jury is eighty percent sure the defendant committed a theft. That is enough for a civil claim based on the same facts, but it might not be enough for a criminal conviction, because the criminal standard asks for a much higher degree of certainty. This difference explains why a person can be acquitted in a criminal trial and still be found liable in a civil one.

lessons.title: Evidence Basics: Relevance, Character and Personal Knowledge
body: Evidence is the information a jury may use to decide a case. The Federal Rules of Evidence, which many states copy in some form, control what comes in. The starting point is relevance. Under Rule 401, evidence is relevant if it makes a fact that matters to the case more or less probable than it would be without the evidence. Under Rule 402, relevant evidence is generally admissible unless a rule says otherwise, and irrelevant evidence is not admissible.

Rule 403 gives the judge power to exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, or wasting time. Unfair prejudice does not mean harmful to a party; all good evidence hurts someone. It means a tendency to lead the jury to decide on an improper basis, such as emotion.

Character evidence is a common trap. Under Rule 404(a), evidence of a person's character is generally not admissible to prove that the person acted in line with it on a particular occasion. A prosecutor generally cannot argue that a defendant is a thief because of earlier thefts. Other bad acts may come in under Rule 404(b) for a purpose other than showing a propensity, such as proving motive, intent, identity, or absence of mistake.

Witnesses must have personal knowledge of what they describe, under Rule 602. A lay witness may offer an opinion only if it is rationally based on perception and helpful, under Rule 701, such as saying a car was going fast. Specialized opinions need an expert qualified under Rule 702. Physical items and documents must be authenticated under Rule 901, meaning there is enough evidence to show the item is what the proponent claims, for example a witness who recognizes the item.

Suppose a defendant is charged with arson and the prosecution wants to show that the defendant bought a gasoline can two days earlier. That is relevant to planning. A photo of the defendant's unrelated, old arrest, offered only to suggest a bad personality, would likely be excluded.

lessons.title: Hearsay and the Confrontation Clause
body: Hearsay is one of the most tested rules in evidence. Under Rule 801(c), hearsay is a statement, other than one the declarant makes while testifying at the current trial, that a party offers to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement. Rule 802 makes hearsay inadmissible unless a rule or statute provides otherwise. The reason is reliability: the person who made the original statement was not under oath and cannot be cross-examined by the jury's own eyes.

The key is purpose. The same words can be hearsay or not, depending on why they are offered. If a witness says "Dana told me the stairs were broken," and the party wants to prove the stairs were broken, that is hearsay. If it is offered only to show that the listener knew about the danger, which affects the listener's state of mind, it is not offered for its truth and is not hearsay. Words that have legal effect themselves, like the words of a contract offer, are also not hearsay.

Some statements are defined as not hearsay. Under Rule 801(d)(2), a statement made by an opposing party and offered against that party is not hearsay. A defendant's own admission, offered by the prosecutor, is the classic example. Other statements fit exceptions that apply whether or not the declarant is available. Under Rule 803, examples include a present sense impression, an excited utterance made under the stress of a startling event, a statement about a then-existing state of mind, statements made for medical diagnosis or treatment, and records of a regularly conducted business activity. Under Rule 804, certain statements, such as former testimony, can be used if the declarant is unavailable.

In criminal cases the Sixth Amendment adds a separate limit. In Crawford v. Washington (2004), the Court held that testimonial statements of an absent witness, such as a formal statement made to police, are not admissible against a defendant unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine. A statement can satisfy a hearsay exception and still violate the Confrontation Clause.

lessons.title: Torts: Negligence and Beyond
body: A tort is a civil wrong, other than breach of contract, for which the law gives a remedy, usually money damages. Torts fall into three broad groups. Intentional torts include battery, which is harmful or offensive contact intended by the defendant, assault, false imprisonment, and trespass to land. Negligence covers harm caused by a failure to use reasonable care. Strict liability makes a defendant liable without proof of fault, for example for harm from abnormally dangerous activities and, in most states, for injuries caused by defective products.

Negligence has four elements. First, the defendant owed the plaintiff a duty of care, usually measured by what a reasonable person would do in the same circumstances. Second, the defendant breached the duty by falling below that standard. Third, the breach caused the harm, which includes actual cause, meaning the harm would not have happened but for the conduct, and proximate cause, meaning the harm was a foreseeable kind of result. Fourth, the plaintiff suffered actual damages. If any element is missing, the plaintiff loses.

Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co. (New York Court of Appeals, 1928) is the famous case on duty and foreseeability. Railroad employees helped a man board a moving train, and he dropped a package of fireworks that exploded, and the shock knocked over scales that injured Mrs. Palsgraf far down the platform. Judge Cardozo wrote for the majority that the railroad owed no duty to a plaintiff who was not within the foreseeable zone of danger. The dissent would have focused instead on whether the conduct was a cause of the harm.

Defenses matter too. If the plaintiff also acted carelessly, most states follow comparative negligence, which reduces the recovery by the plaintiff's share of fault, with some barring recovery if the plaintiff is more than fifty percent at fault. A small minority of states and the District of Columbia keep contributory negligence, under which even slight plaintiff fault can bar recovery. Consent and assumption of risk can also reduce or bar a claim.

lessons.title: Contracts: Formation, Defenses and Remedies
body: A contract is a promise or set of promises the law will enforce. Formation requires mutual assent, usually shown by an offer and an acceptance, and consideration, which is a bargained-for exchange of something of legal value. Courts judge assent objectively, by what a reasonable person would understand from the parties' words and conduct, not by secret intentions. In Lucy v. Zehmer (Virginia, 1954), a farm owner who wrote a sale on a restaurant check, claiming it was a joke, was held to the deal because a reasonable person in the buyer's position would think it serious.

Two bodies of law govern most contracts. The common law, summarized in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, covers services, land, and most other subjects. Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code, which states have adopted in some form, covers sales of goods and relaxes some common-law formality rules, for example by allowing a contract even if some terms are left open. Certain contracts, including those for the sale of land and many contracts that cannot be performed within a year, must be in writing to be enforceable, under the statute of frauds.

A party can attack a contract with defenses. These include lack of capacity, which is why minors can generally cancel contracts, misrepresentation, duress, and unconscionability, meaning terms so one-sided and unfairly imposed that a court will not enforce them. Even without a defense, a promise without consideration may be enforced in some cases under promissory estoppel, which protects reasonable reliance on a clear promise.

If one side breaches, the usual remedy is damages that give the non-breaching party the benefit of the bargain, called expectation damages. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) limits recovery for consequential losses to those that were foreseeable to the breaching party when the contract was made. In that case a mill owner could not recover lost profits because the carrier had no notice that the delay would stop the mill. In rare cases, such as for unique property like land, a court may order specific performance instead.

lessons.title: Students' Free Speech Rights
body: The First Amendment applies in public schools, but courts balance it against a school's need to teach and keep order. The foundation is Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969). Students who wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War were suspended. The Supreme Court held that students do not lose their rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate. A school may restrict student speech only if it can reasonably forecast that it will materially and substantially disrupt school activities or invade the rights of others. Fear or dislike of an unpopular view is not enough. An earlier case, West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943), held that a school cannot force students to salute the flag.

Later cases carved out categories. In Bethel School District No. 403 v. Fraser (1986), the Court held that a school may punish lewd and vulgar speech at a school assembly, because schools have an interest in teaching civil discourse. In Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier (1988), it held that schools may exercise editorial control over school-sponsored expression, such as a student newspaper produced as part of a class, as long as their actions are reasonably related to legitimate educational concerns. In Morse v. Frederick (2007), the Court held that a school may restrict student speech at a school-supervised event that it reasonably views as promoting illegal drug use, in a case involving a banner at a parade across from a school.

The newest major case is Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021). A student who failed to make the varsity cheerleading team posted a crude message on social media from off campus, and the school suspended her from junior varsity. The Court held that the school violated her First Amendment rights. It did not say that schools can never regulate off-campus speech. It said that a school's interest is weaker off campus and listed situations, such as serious bullying or threats, where it may still act.
A useful method is to ask three questions: Is the speech personal or school-sponsored? Did it happen at school or elsewhere? Did it cause or threaten real disruption, or was it just offensive?

lessons.title: Searches, Discipline and Due Process at School
body: The Fourth Amendment protects students from unreasonable searches by school officials, but the standard is relaxed. In New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985), a teacher found a student smoking in a bathroom, and the assistant principal opened her purse and found cigarettes, rolling papers and evidence of marijuana dealing. The Court held that school officials do not need a warrant or probable cause. A search is lawful if it is justified at its start by reasonable grounds for suspecting that it will turn up evidence that the student has violated the law or school rules, and if the search is reasonably related in scope to its purpose and not excessively intrusive given the student's age and sex and the nature of the infraction.

The limits of that test appeared in Safford Unified School District No. 1 v. Redding (2009). School officials strip-searched a thirteen-year-old girl on a tip that she had prescription-strength ibuprofen. The Court held that the search was unreasonable, because the suspected items posed little danger and there was no reason to think they were hidden in her underwear.

Drug testing is a different category. In Vernonia School District 47J v. Acton (1995), the Court upheld random drug testing of student athletes, reasoning that students have a reduced expectation of privacy, that the intrusion was limited, and that the school had an important interest in deterring drug use among athletes. Later, in Board of Education v. Earls (2002), it extended the approach to students in competitive extracurricular activities.

Due process also applies to discipline. In Goss v. Lopez (1975), the Court held that a public school student facing a short suspension has a protected interest in education and is entitled to notice of the charges and an opportunity to tell his or her side. The process can be informal and quick for a suspension of ten days or less. Longer suspensions and expulsions generally call for more.
These cases mostly concern public schools, because the Constitution limits government actors. Private schools set rules through their contracts and handbooks.

lessons.title: Young People in the Justice System
body: Juvenile courts began in the early twentieth century with a rehabilitative philosophy and informal procedures. By the 1960s critics argued that young people received neither the care of a caring system nor the protections of a criminal one. In re Gault (1967) responded. A fifteen-year-old in Arizona was sent to a state industrial school for up to six years, without notice of the charges, a lawyer, or the chance to confront the complainant. The Supreme Court held that in a delinquency proceeding that may result in commitment, due process requires adequate notice, the right to counsel, the right to confront and cross-examine witnesses, and the privilege against self-incrimination. In re Winship (1970) added the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard. But McKeiver v. Pennsylvania (1971) held that the Constitution does not require a jury trial in juvenile delinquency proceedings, so many states use a judge.

The Court has also recognized that youth matters in other ways. In J.D.B. v. North Carolina (2011), it held that a child's age is relevant to whether the child is in custody for Miranda purposes, when a reasonable child would not feel free to leave.

On sentencing, the Eighth Amendment bars cruel and unusual punishments, and the Court has said that its meaning draws on evolving standards of decency. In Roper v. Simmons (2005), the Court held that the death penalty cannot be imposed for crimes committed by people under eighteen. In Graham v. Florida (2010), it held that life without parole cannot be imposed on a juvenile for a crime other than homicide. In Miller v. Alabama (2012), it held that mandatory life without parole for juveniles convicted of homicide violates the Eighth Amendment, so sentencers must be able to consider youth and its circumstances. The Court's reasoning rests on research and common sense that young people are more impulsive, more influenced by peers, and more capable of change.

People still disagree about how to treat serious youth offenses. Some stress accountability and protection of victims, while others stress developmental differences and rehabilitation. The cases above set constitutional floors, and states choose how to go beyond them.

lessons.title: How a Mock Trial Works
body: A mock trial is a simulated trial in which teams of students act as lawyers and witnesses before a judge, often a real attorney or judge volunteering. Programs differ in their rules, so always read your competition's rules and case packet. Most follow the same arc. The case packet gives the stipulated facts, the witness statements, exhibits, and a simplified set of rules of evidence, often adapted from the Federal Rules of Evidence. Both sides prepare to argue either side of the case, and a team usually appears for the prosecution or plaintiff in one round and for the defense in another.

The typical order of a trial is opening statements by each side, then the case of the party with the burden, which is the prosecution in a criminal case or the plaintiff in a civil one. Each witness is examined on direct by the calling side, cross-examined by the opponent, and sometimes questioned again on redirect and recross. Then the defense presents its case in the same way, and each side gives a closing argument. In many formats the party with the burden of proof speaks last in closing.

The key to winning is a theory of the case. A theory is a short, believable story that explains the facts in a way that leads to your result and fits the law. For example, a defense theory in a theft case might be: "This is a case of mistaken identity." Every choice you make should connect back to the theory: which witnesses to call, which questions to ask, and what to emphasize in closing. A strong theory is simple, rests on facts in the packet, and answers the other side's best points.

Team roles include attorneys, witnesses, and often timekeepers and bailiffs. Witnesses must stay within their written statements. They may not invent facts that harm or help their side, though in many formats they may be asked about reasonable details not covered. Honesty with the rules matters as much as skill.

lessons.title: Opening Statements and Direct Examination
body: An opening statement is a preview. It is not an argument. You tell the judge or jury what the case is about, what the evidence will show, and why your side should win. Because an opening is a promise, you must not promise anything you cannot prove. Good openings begin with a clear theme, introduce the people, walk through events in order, and tell the fact finder what verdict you will ask for. Avoid legal conclusions presented as facts, and avoid arguing. Phrases like "the evidence will show" help keep you on the right side of that line.

Direct examination is when your own witness testifies. Its purpose is to let the witness tell the story, so the questions must be open and non-leading. A leading question suggests the answer, such as "You saw the defendant run, didn't you?" Under Federal Rule of Evidence 611(c), leading questions are generally not allowed on direct, except for preliminary matters or when a witness has trouble communicating. A proper question is "What did you see?" or "What happened next?"

Organize direct testimony around a clear structure. Begin by introducing the witness, with background that makes the witness believable. Then set the scene, move through events in a natural order, and finish strong, ending on the most important point. Use short, simple questions that call for one fact at a time. Lead the witness into new topics with transitional phrases such as "Let's turn to the evening of March 3."

Witnesses may testify only about what they personally perceived, under Rule 602. To introduce an exhibit, lay a foundation: have the witness identify the item, explain how they know it, and confirm that it is a fair and accurate copy. Then ask the court to admit it. Skipping foundation is a common reason an objection is sustained.

Practice matters. Witnesses should listen to the question, answer only that question, and stay truthful to their statements. Lawyers should know the answers they expect to hear, because direct is a planned conversation, not a surprise.

lessons.title: Cross-Examination and Impeachment
body: Cross-examination is questioning the opposing side's witness. Its goals are modest and specific: to get helpful facts from the witness, to show gaps or weaknesses in the story, and to cast doubt on the witness's reliability. It is not the place to argue with the witness or to ask the witness to explain.

The main tool is the leading question, which Rule 611(c) allows on cross. A good leading question makes one simple factual statement that the witness can only confirm, such as "You were standing forty feet away." Chain several such statements to build a point. Rule 611(b) also generally limits cross to the subject matter of the direct and to the witness's credibility, though a court may allow more. A classic rule of thumb is never to ask a question when you do not already know the answer, and never to ask the witness "why," because that invites a speech.

Impeachment means attacking credibility. There are several methods. The simplest is a prior inconsistent statement under Rule 613: you commit the witness to the testimony, credit the earlier statement by showing it was made at a reliable time, and then confront the witness with the contradiction. Another method is showing bias or motive, such as a friendship or a financial stake. A third is showing poor ability to perceive, such as bad lighting, distance, or poor eyesight. Rule 608 allows asking about specific instances of untruthful conduct, and Rule 609 allows certain criminal convictions to be used, subject to conditions.

Suppose a witness testified on direct that she clearly saw the driver's face. On cross, you might ask: it was nighttime, the streetlight was out, you were across the road, it lasted about two seconds, and you gave the police a description that did not mention a beard. Each question is short, each is a fact, and together they undermine the identification without arguing.
Be respectful. Judges and jurors dislike aggressive questioning, and a calm cross often works better than a loud one. When you have made your points, sit down.

lessons.title: Objections
body: An objection is a formal protest that a question, answer, or exhibit breaks a rule of evidence or procedure. Objections protect the record and the fairness of the trial. To object, stand, say "Objection," and state a short, specific ground, such as "Objection, hearsay." Do not argue until the judge invites you. The judge then rules by saying "sustained," which means the objection is accepted, or "overruled," which means it is rejected. If you are the other side, you may be asked to respond, and you should briefly say why the evidence is allowed.

Some objections are about the form of the question. Leading, which suggests the answer, is improper on direct but allowed on cross. Compound questions ask two things at once. Argumentative questions quarrel with the witness instead of seeking facts. Asked and answered objects to repeating a question. Vague questions are unclear, and assumes facts not in evidence objects to a question that slips in an unproven fact, such as "When did you stop stealing?"

Others are about substance. Relevance objects that the evidence does not tend to prove a fact that matters, under Rules 401 and 402. Hearsay objects that an out-of-court statement is offered for its truth, under Rule 802. Lack of foundation, or lack of personal knowledge under Rule 602, objects that the witness has not shown how they know. Improper opinion under Rule 701 objects to a lay witness's speculation. Improper character evidence under Rule 404 objects to using someone's character to show conduct on a particular occasion. Privilege objects to forcing disclosure of protected communications, such as those with a lawyer.

Timing matters. Object promptly, before the answer if you can. If you are late, ask to strike the answer. Do not object so often that you annoy the judge or interrupt the flow, because each objection should have a real purpose. When the opponent objects to your question, you can cure many problems by rephrasing, for example by asking an open question in place of a leading one, or by laying foundation first.
A good practice drill: take each question in a witness script and ask what objection the other side might raise, and how you would answer.

lessons.title: Closing Arguments and Courtroom Ethics
body: The closing argument is the one time you may openly argue. You review the evidence, tie it to the law, and ask for a verdict. You may argue reasonable inferences from the evidence, point out contradictions, and explain why your witnesses should be believed. You may not state facts that were never proven, refer to evidence the court excluded, or give your own personal opinion about guilt or credibility in a way that suggests private knowledge.

A strong closing follows a clear structure. Begin with your theme in a sentence or two. Walk through the elements the law requires and show, with citations to testimony and exhibits, how the evidence meets them, or in the defense's case, how the other side fell short. Address the opponent's best points directly instead of hiding from them. In a criminal case, a defense closing often stresses that the prosecution has the burden to prove each element beyond a reasonable doubt. A prosecutor's closing, by contrast, must show that the evidence fits together to satisfy that high standard. End with a specific request, such as "ask you to return a verdict of not guilty."

In many mock trial formats the party with the burden gives a rebuttal. Rebuttal is limited to answering what the opponent said, not introducing new points. Keep an eye on time limits, since going over often costs points.

Ethics are part of the activity because they are part of real law. Real lawyers are bound by rules of professional conduct, which in most states follow the American Bar Association's Model Rules of Professional Conduct. Examples include the duty of confidentiality in Rule 1.6 and the duty of candor to the tribunal in Rule 3.3, which forbids knowingly making false statements of fact or law to the court. Lawyers also have duties to be competent and to avoid conflicts of interest.

In mock trial, the equivalent is honesty and good sportsmanship. Do not make up facts, do not coach witnesses to depart from their statements, and treat opponents and the court with respect. Winning on integrity matters more than winning a round.

lessons.title: Legal Careers and the Path In
body: Law offers many careers, and only some involve a courtroom. Lawyers who litigate argue cases, but many lawyers are transactional, drafting contracts, advising on deals, and helping clients plan. Prosecutors represent the government in criminal cases, and public defenders represent defendants who cannot afford a lawyer. Legal aid organizations help people with limited income in matters like housing and benefits. In-house counsel work inside businesses. Government lawyers advise agencies and write regulations, and legislative staff help draft statutes. Judges decide cases, and in most states and the federal system they are lawyers first. Mediators and arbitrators help parties resolve disputes outside court. Paralegals and legal assistants support lawyers by researching, organizing documents, and preparing cases, and they do not need to be lawyers, though they may not give legal advice or represent clients in court in the ordinary case.

The usual path to becoming a lawyer in the United States begins with a bachelor's degree in any subject. Students then attend law school, which typically takes three years and awards the Juris Doctor, or J.D. Most states require graduation from a law school approved by the American Bar Association for admission to the bar, though a few states allow other routes. Law schools generally consider an applicant's grades and standardized test results, and the rules and tests can change, so check current requirements. After law school, graduates take a state bar examination and a character and fitness review. A lawyer is licensed by a state, and many states also require continuing legal education and follow professional conduct rules based on the ABA Model Rules.

High school students can prepare in several ways. Reading, writing, and speaking skills are central, so debate, mock trial, and writing-intensive classes help. Volunteering at courts or legal clinics, where allowed, can show what the work looks like. Skills like analysis, listening, and clear communication matter in every legal job.

Law is also a path to public service and to work in many fields that touch the law, such as policy, journalism, compliance, and business. Costs and debt are real considerations, and choosing a career should weigh interests, values, and finances.

lessons.title: Sources of International Law and the UN System
body: International law governs relations among states and certain other international actors. It has no world legislature or police, so it depends on consent and on shared interest. A standard list of its sources appears in Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The main sources are treaties, which bind the states that are party to them, international custom, which is general state practice accepted as law, and general principles of law recognized by nations. Judicial decisions and the writings of highly qualified scholars are subsidiary means for identifying the rules.

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) sets rules for how treaties are made, interpreted, and ended. Its core principle is pacta sunt servanda, that every treaty in force is binding on the parties and must be performed in good faith. A state generally cannot excuse breach by pointing to its own domestic law. The Convention also recognizes peremptory norms, called jus cogens, which are rules from which no derogation is permitted, such as the prohibition of genocide. The United States has signed but not ratified the Convention, though it treats many of its provisions as reflecting customary law.

The United Nations was founded in 1945 under the Charter of the United Nations. Article 2(4) of the Charter requires members to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. There are two widely accepted exceptions: the inherent right of self-defense recognized in Article 51 if an armed attack occurs, and action authorized by the Security Council under Chapter VII. How far self-defense extends, for example against threats that have not yet occurred, is debated among states and scholars.

The International Court of Justice at The Hague decides disputes between states that have accepted its jurisdiction, by special agreement, treaty clause, or declaration, and gives advisory opinions to UN organs. Its judgments bind the parties, but it has no enforcement police. The International Criminal Court, created by the Rome Statute of 1998, prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and aggression. It has jurisdiction in limited circumstances, and several major powers, including the United States, are not parties to the Statute. Its authority is disputed by some governments.

lessons.title: Human Rights Law and Treaties at Home
body: Modern human rights law grew from the Second World War. In 1948 the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which sets out civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. As a General Assembly declaration it was not itself a treaty, but it has been very influential, and many scholars argue that parts of it now reflect customary law. Two treaties followed in 1966: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. The United States ratified the first in 1992, with reservations, and has signed but not ratified the second. Other core treaties address genocide, racial discrimination, discrimination against women, torture, and children. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) has been ratified by nearly every state, and the United States has signed but not ratified it.

There are also regional systems. The European Convention on Human Rights (1950) is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, where individuals can bring complaints against member states. The Americas and Africa have commissions and courts of their own. International humanitarian law, which governs armed conflict, is a related field, found chiefly in the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their protocols. It protects people not taking part in hostilities, such as civilians, the wounded, and prisoners of war.

How a treaty operates inside the United States depends on the Constitution. The President negotiates treaties, and the Senate must give advice and consent by a two-thirds vote. A ratified treaty is part of the supreme law of the land under Article VI, but courts distinguish between self-executing treaties, which can be enforced directly by courts, and non-self-executing treaties, which require implementing legislation. In Medellin v. Texas (2008), the Supreme Court held that a judgment of the International Court of Justice about consular notification was not directly enforceable as domestic law in the state courts without action by Congress.

People disagree about the weight of international human rights law. Supporters argue that universal standards check abuse and protect vulnerable people. Critics argue that some bodies lack democratic accountability, and that national constitutions and elected legislatures should have the final say. Both views are part of the real debate over treaties.

questions.prompt: Which of these sources of law ranks highest in the United States?
choices: The United States Constitution
A local city ordinance
A regulation written by a federal agency
A statute passed by a state legislature

questions.prompt: What does stare decisis tell a court to do?
choices: Defer to the legislature before deciding any question of law
Follow earlier decisions on the same legal issue in its own system
Ignore earlier decisions whenever the facts are slightly different
Apply the law of whichever state the plaintiff lives in

questions.prompt: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), what power did the Supreme Court recognize for itself?
choices: The power to write the budget for the executive branch
The power to veto a bill that Congress had passed
The power to strike down unconstitutional laws
The power to remove a President who breaks the law

questions.prompt: A state enacts a law that conflicts with a valid federal statute passed under Congress's constitutional powers, on the same subject. A business asks which governs. Which analysis is most accurate?
choices: The older of the two laws controls regardless of source
The state law governs because states have a general police power
Neither governs, and the matter must be sent to a local court
The federal statute controls where the two conflict

questions.prompt: Which Article of the Constitution vests executive power in the President?
choices: Article III
Article IV
Article I
Article II

questions.prompt: What vote in each chamber does Congress need to override a presidential veto?
choices: A simple majority of members present and voting
Three fifths of the members of each chamber
Two thirds of the members of each chamber
Three fourths of the members of each chamber

questions.prompt: What did the Court hold in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)?
choices: The President could seize steel mills during a threatened strike
The President lacked authority to seize the mills
Congress could not regulate the steel industry in any way
The courts had no power to review actions by a President

questions.prompt: Congress passes a statute banning the President from sending troops to a specific region. The President orders troops there anyway, and a lawsuit follows. Using Justice Jackson's framework from Youngstown, where does the President's claim fall?
choices: Weakest, since the President acts against Congress
Strongest, because the President has authority from Congress
Uncertain, because Congress has been silent on the issue
Strongest, because the executive acts alone in foreign affairs

questions.prompt: Which amendment makes most of the Bill of Rights applicable to the states through due process?
choices: The Fifth Amendment
The Eleventh Amendment (suits against states)
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment

questions.prompt: What did Barron v. Baltimore (1833) hold?
choices: The Bill of Rights restricts both the federal and state governments
The states may not tax federal banks at all
The Constitution does not protect free speech anywhere
The Bill of Rights restricts only the federal government

questions.prompt: A state police officer conducts an unreasonable search and finds evidence. Under Mapp v. Ohio (1961), what is the likely result in the state criminal trial?
choices: The evidence is excluded under the exclusionary rule
The evidence is admitted but the jury must be warned
The evidence is admitted because the officer found it
The evidence is admitted because states are not bound by the Fourth Amendment

questions.prompt: A city bans all handgun possession in the home, with no exception, and a resident challenges it citing the Second Amendment. Based on Heller (2008) as described in this lesson, what is the strongest argument for the resident?
choices: Heller held that the Second Amendment applies only in federal territory
Heller recognized an individual right to keep a handgun at home
Heller held that cities may ban any firearm they choose
Heller held that the Second Amendment protects only militia members

questions.prompt: Which amendment reserves powers not given to the nation to the states or the people?
choices: The Fourth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment

questions.prompt: What was the outcome in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)?
choices: Congress could charter a national bank, and a state could not tax it
Congress lacked power to charter a bank, and states could tax it
Congress could charter a bank, but states could tax it freely
Congress lacked power to charter a bank, but states could not tax it

questions.prompt: Why did the Court in United States v. Lopez (1995) strike down the Gun-Free School Zones Act?
choices: Firearms are protected by the First Amendment because carrying one is a form of expression
Congress has no power to pass any law about the safety of schools
The Tenth Amendment forbids Congress from passing any gun law at all
Carrying a gun near a school was not economic and was too weakly tied to commerce

questions.prompt: Congress passes a statute ordering every state legislature to enact a particular licensing law for private businesses. Under the anti-commandeering principle recognized in Murphy v. NCAA (2018), what is the most likely outcome of a challenge by a state?
choices: The statute is invalid because Congress can regulate only federal employees
The statute stands because the Supremacy Clause lets Congress order states
The statute is invalid because Congress cannot commandeer states
The statute stands because licensing is an enumerated federal power

questions.prompt: Which court generally decides most disputes between private parties over state-law matters?
choices: A state trial court
A federal court of appeals
The United States Supreme Court
The International Court of Justice

questions.prompt: What are the two main routes to federal jurisdiction described in this lesson?
choices: Presidential order and legislative request
Federal question and diversity of citizenship
Plaintiff's choice and defendant's consent
Appeal from a state court and a referendum

questions.prompt: A resident of Ohio sues a Michigan company for $200,000 over a contract in federal court. What does Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938) require the federal court to apply?
choices: The law of the plaintiff's home country
A uniform national contract code written by Congress
State substantive law
Federal common law on contracts

questions.prompt: A citizen of Texas sues a citizen of Texas in federal court over an unpaid $500,000 loan. The loan is governed only by state law. What is the best description of the court's jurisdiction?
choices: It may hear the case if the defendant agrees to waive jurisdiction
It may hear the case under diversity because the amount exceeds $75,000
It may hear the case because all contracts are federal questions
It lacks jurisdiction: no federal question and no diversity

questions.prompt: What document begins a civil lawsuit?
choices: A subpoena duces tecum
A verdict form
An indictment
A complaint

questions.prompt: A defendant files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. What question does the court ask?
choices: Whether the plaintiff has completed all discovery
Whether the defendant's witnesses are more credible than the plaintiff's
Whether the law gives a remedy if the complaint's facts are true
Whether the jury would find in the plaintiff's favor at trial

questions.prompt: Which statement describes summary judgment under Rule 56?
choices: It is granted whenever one party has more evidence than the other
It is granted when no material fact is genuinely disputed
It is granted whenever the judge thinks the defendant's witness is more believable
It is granted automatically if discovery is not complete

questions.prompt: After discovery, the plaintiff's own deposition and the defendant's records conflict about whether a payment was ever made, and both are supported by sworn testimony. The defendant moves for summary judgment. What is the most likely ruling?
choices: Denied, since a material fact is genuinely disputed
Denied, because summary judgment is available only to plaintiffs
Granted, because documents always outweigh testimony
Granted, because the defendant filed the motion first

questions.prompt: What standard generally supports a lawful arrest or a warrant?
choices: Preponderance of the evidence
A hunch that something is wrong
Probable cause
Proof beyond a reasonable doubt

questions.prompt: What did Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) hold?
choices: Police must read warnings before every conversation with a suspect
Defendants may not be tried twice for the same offense in any court
Juries must be unanimous in all state misdemeanor cases
States must provide counsel to felony defendants who cannot pay

questions.prompt: Which describes the situation in which Miranda warnings are required?
choices: Custodial interrogation of a suspect
Only when a suspect is arrested for a felony
Whenever police talk to anyone about a crime
Only after a defendant has been convicted

questions.prompt: Police stop Lena on the street and ask where she was last night. She is not under arrest and may walk away. She says she was near the store that was robbed. At trial, she argues that the statement must be excluded because she was not given Miranda warnings. What is the best analysis?
choices: Excluded, because any statement to police requires a lawyer
Admissible, because Miranda requires custody and she had none
Admissible, because Miranda applies only to written statements
Excluded, because Miranda applies whenever police ask any question

questions.prompt: Which standard of proof is lowest?
choices: Clear and convincing evidence
Preponderance of the evidence
Proof to a moral certainty
Beyond a reasonable doubt

questions.prompt: What did In re Winship (1970) hold?
choices: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt is required in delinquency cases
Preponderance of the evidence is enough in juvenile delinquency cases
Juveniles have a constitutional right to a jury in delinquency cases
Clear and convincing evidence is required in all civil cases

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the burden of persuasion and the burden of production?
choices: Both are the same duty and always rest on the same party at trial
Persuasion applies only to judges while production applies only to juries
Persuasion is the duty to present some evidence, production is the duty to convince
Persuasion is about convincing, production is about offering enough evidence

questions.prompt: A jury in a civil case believes it is about seventy percent likely that a defendant took a ring, and it is a case in which the plaintiff must prove the claim by a preponderance. Separately, the state prosecutes the same defendant for theft. What is the most accurate statement?
choices: The criminal case needs only a preponderance because the facts are the same
The civil result is invalid unless the criminal trial also convicts
A preponderance may be met, but conviction needs much more certainty
Both cases require the same certainty, so the results must match

questions.prompt: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 401, evidence is relevant if it does what?
choices: Makes a fact of consequence more or less probable
Comes from a person qualified as an expert in the subject matter
Is recorded in a written document that was signed by someone
Proves a fact of the case beyond any reasonable doubt at all

questions.prompt: A prosecutor offers the defendant's old, unrelated conviction only to suggest that he is a dishonest person who probably committed the charged theft. What is the most likely objection?
choices: Best evidence rule for documents
Improper character evidence
Lack of personal knowledge by the witness
Privilege against self-incrimination

questions.prompt: What is the standard under Rule 403 for excluding relevant evidence?
choices: It is more probable than not that the jury will dislike it intensely
It was not mentioned in the opening statements of either lawyer
Its probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice
It hurts the case of one of the parties in the trial more than the other side

questions.prompt: In an arson trial, the prosecution calls a hardware store clerk who identifies a receipt as the one she gave the defendant for a gasoline can two days before the fire. The defense objects to the receipt. Which response is strongest?
choices: The receipt is hearsay, so it is admitted for that reason
The receipt is character evidence, so it is admitted for that reason
The clerk lacks knowledge, so it is admitted for that reason
It is relevant to planning and the clerk authenticated it

questions.prompt: Under Rule 801(c), hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered for what purpose?
choices: To establish who the speaker was in the room
To impeach a lawyer's closing argument
To prove the truth of the matter asserted
To show how the listener reacted afterward

questions.prompt: A party offers the opposing party's own earlier statement against that party. How does Rule 801(d)(2) treat it?
choices: It is inadmissible hearsay without exception
It is admissible only if the party is unavailable
It is admissible only if made under oath
It is not hearsay when offered against that party

choices: Not hearsay, since it is offered for its effect on the listener
Hearsay, because the neighbor is not a party to the case
Not hearsay, because statements about stairs are never offered for their truth
Hearsay, because every out-of-court statement is hearsay

questions.prompt: A bystander makes a formal statement to a police officer describing a stabbing, and then cannot be found for trial. The prosecution offers the statement against the defendant, and the defendant never had a chance to cross-examine the bystander. Under Crawford v. Washington (2004), what is the most likely result?
choices: Admissible, because the statement was made to a police officer
Excluded, because it is testimonial and was never cross-examined
Excluded, because statements made to police are always irrelevant
Admissible, because the bystander is unavailable to testify in person

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT an element of negligence?
choices: Actual and proximate cause
A duty of care
Breach of the duty
Intent to harm

questions.prompt: What is the difference between actual cause and proximate cause?
choices: Actual cause is foreseeability and proximate cause is the but-for test
Actual cause concerns damages and proximate cause concerns duty
Actual cause is the but-for link; proximate cause is foreseeability
They are two names for the same requirement

choices: $100,000, because the defendant was also at fault
$60,000, the defendant's share of the fault
Nothing, because any fault by the plaintiff bars recovery
$40,000, which is the plaintiff's share of the fault

choices: It owed Rosa no duty, since she was outside the zone of danger
The railroad was strictly liable for any explosion on its premises
Rosa assumed the risk by standing on a train platform

questions.prompt: Which body of law governs contracts for the sale of goods?
choices: UCC Article 2 on sales of goods
The Federal Rules of Evidence
The Model Penal Code

questions.prompt: What is the usual goal of expectation damages?
choices: To return the parties to their positions before the contract
To give the non-breaching party the benefit of the bargain
To force the breaching party to perform the contract
To punish the breaching party

choices: The mill owner was a minor and so could not bring any lawsuit
Lost profits are never recoverable in any contract case anywhere
The carrier could not foresee that a delay would stop the mill
Contracts for carrying goods can never support any damages for delay

choices: Max is not bound, because a check cannot contain a contract
Max is bound, because every written note is automatically a contract
Max is not bound, because his private intent controls

questions.prompt: In Tinker (1969), students were suspended for wearing what?

Black armbands
Buttons supporting a candidate

West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

choices: The First Amendment does not apply at all to speech made on social media
Schools may never regulate any speech that a student makes off campus at all
Schools may always regulate off-campus speech exactly like on-campus speech

Fraser, because the article was lewd speech at an assembly
Hazelwood, since the paper is school-sponsored

choices: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt
Probable cause and a signed warrant from a judge
Reasonable suspicion and reasonable scope

A school nurse was not present to supervise or witness the search

A hearing before a federal judge

The policy is struck down, because testing without individual suspicion is never allowed
